newsitem.title: USA: Andersons CEO sees less vomitoxin concern.
newsitem.headline: Andersons CEO sees less vomitoxin concern.

text.p: Vomitoxin problems with new crop soft red winter wheat may be less of a concern than originally feared, Richard Anderson, chairman and chief executive officer of The Andersons Inc, said.
"The feeling right now is that it's less of an issue than we had been concerned about, which is good news. But we don't know yet how it's all going to play out," he told Reuters.

The Maumee, Ohio-based company, which has grain elevators and other agricultural businesses, in July posted vomitoxin price discounts on bids for new crop soft red winter wheat but a week later reduced the discount schedule.

Vomitoxin, a toxin produced by the fungus disease scab or head blight in wheat, can be potentially poisonous to both humans and livestock. The Food and Drug Administration advises maximum limits of one part per million for wheat aimed at human consumption, 10 ppm for cattle and five ppm for hogs.

Anderson said that his company, with 67 million bushels of grain storage, invested "quite a bit" in thorough testing and took a "pretty conservative position... We lost some market share because of that conservatism, but we didn't want to be caught with a lot of wheat that we owned when we weren't sure of its value in the marketplace," he said.
Anderson said the first shipments of affected wheat sold into foreign markets "seem to be going OK" although it's difficult to get consistency in sampling and in testing.
"The tests at destination are (showing) less incidence of vomitoxin than the tests that we had as we loaded the vessel," he said.

He did not specify pricing but said he is comfortable with it. "We're realizing a reasonable price on the outbound side," he said. On Andersons's purchases from farmers, he said, "we were very conservative on the inbound so we're safe so far as what we've bought."
